Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing quite symbolizes true love like the release of caged butterflies, does it? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are reportedly set to receive $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding, with the butterfly release said to be the pièce de résistance of England's most anticipated celebrity nuptials of the year. Wayne Rooney, widely regarded as the finest English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his high school sweetheart, were to be married Thursday in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy. As the couple kiss, guests are apparently expected to open boxes and release the butterflies into the air.

This moment has been roundly mocked in the British media—dismissed as tacky and excessive—though one wonders whether such criticism amounts to little more than sour grapes. The couple's path to the altar has been a long and, at times, turbulent one, marked by relentless criticism from a press that has seemed to delight in portraying Rooney and McLoughlin as "common." The Daily Mail once went so far as to ask: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been derisively nicknamed "Shrek" and "Mr. Potato Head" on account of his appearance, while his background as the son of a school dinner lady, raised on a council estate, is frequently invoked in a disparaging tone. McLoughlin, for her part, has endured countless unflattering stories about her weight, her shopping habits, and her perceived lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. She has also faced sharp criticism for having become a millionaire in her own right—an achievement the press seems eager to attribute entirely to Rooney, rather than to her own evident decency, academic success in school, and shrewd ability to translate her fame into media and advertising ventures. Anyone who has watched her television program, Coleen's Real Women, can attest that she is warm, down-to-earth, and remarkably skilled at putting others at ease.

Much to the media's chagrin, the couple sold the exclusive rights to cover their wedding to OK! magazine for a record $5 million. Yet they are not keeping the entire sum for themselves: an undisclosed portion of the fee will be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister, Rosie, receives care. By contrast, when the Queen's grandson, Peter Phillips, and his bride, Autumn Kelly, recently accepted $1 million from Hello! magazine to cover their wedding, they faced only a fraction of the scorn now directed at the far more generous—if less privileged—Rooney and McLoughlin. In addition, rather than requesting traditional gifts, the couple have asked guests to make donations to Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool.

The wedding may well be extravagant, complete with a private yacht, a luxury jet for guests (whose expenses the couple are covering), fine wine, and a $200,000 gown—but at the very least, this is a couple who has earned what they now enjoy through hard work. Indeed, their success despite working-class origins appears to be precisely what irritates critics most. There seems to be an unspoken rule that those not born into privilege, and who never attended elite schools, should somehow be denied the pleasure of their own prosperity—as though such enjoyment were itself unseemly. If anything, the couple's relationship and achievements represent a triumph over adversity. The two have known each other since McLoughlin was twelve, though she spent two years rebuffing Rooney's attempts to ask her out. He finally seized his opportunity upon seeing her struggling with a broken bicycle chain; he rode over to assist her, renewed his proposal for a date, and this time received a yes.

Surely, then, they deserve to be congratulated for crafting their own modern-day fairy tale—butterflies and all.

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

# A Fairytale Wedding Under Fire

Is there anything more romantic than freeing butterflies from their cages? At least, that's what Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin seem to believe—the release of these winged creatures is expected to be the grand finale of what's being called the year's most-watched celebrity wedding in England, for which the couple has secured a $5 million deal covering photography rights.

Set to marry Thursday in an Italian ceremony reportedly costing $10 million, England's premier footballer of his generation and his childhood sweetheart planned for guests to unleash the butterflies as the newlyweds shared their first kiss. This moment has drawn widespread mockery from British media outlets, who've dismissed it as tasteless and excessive. But one has to wonder—is this genuine criticism, or simple envy?

The journey to this altar hasn't been smooth for the pair. They've endured relentless scrutiny from British tabloids, which seem to relish portraying Rooney and McLoughlin as unrefined. One notably harsh headline from the Daily Mail questioned whether they might be "Britain's ghastliest couple." Rooney's appearance has earned him unflattering nicknames like "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head," while his working-class roots—raised by a school cafeteria worker on public housing—are frequently mentioned with a condescending tone.

McLoughlin hasn't fared better, facing endless tabloid coverage criticizing her weight, spending habits, and supposed distance from Victoria Beckham. Critics have also taken aim at her independent financial success, insisting it stems entirely from her relationship with Rooney rather than acknowledging her own merits—her academic achievements, her genuine likability, and her savvy in building media and advertising ventures. Those familiar with her program, Coleen's Real Women, would recognize her as warm, genuine, and skilled at making others comfortable.

Adding fuel to the media's outrage, the couple sold exclusive wedding coverage rights to OK magazine for an unprecedented $5 million. Yet they aren't keeping every penny—a portion of that sum will go to Claire House, a children's hospice in Cheshire that cares for McLoughlin's foster sister Rosie, who has disabilities.

Consider the contrast: when the Queen's grandson Peter Phillips wed Autumn Kelly, they accepted roughly $1 million from Hello magazine for similar coverage, yet faced nowhere near the level of criticism now aimed at Rooney and McLoughlin—despite the latter couple being more charitable and coming from humbler origins. The pair has additionally requested that wedding guests contribute to Liverpool's Alder Hey children's hospital instead of giving traditional gifts.

Yes, the celebration includes lavish touches—a private yacht, chartered jets for attendees (all expenses covered by the couple), fine wine, and a wedding gown reportedly worth $200,000. Still, this couple earned their fortune through their own efforts. Perhaps what truly irritates critics is precisely this: that people without privileged backgrounds or elite educations have managed to build substantial wealth and now enjoy it freely. Apparently, that's considered unacceptable—almost offensive.

In truth, their story represents a genuine triumph over hardship. The two have known each other since McLoughlin was just 12 years old, though she resisted his attempts to ask her out for two full years. His breakthrough moment came when he spotted her wrestling with a jammed bicycle chain, rode to her rescue, and finally received the yes he'd been hoping for.

Doesn't this couple deserve recognition for crafting their own contemporary fairytale, butterflies included?

*The opinions expressed in this commentary belong solely to the author.*

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin decided to tie the knot, their union became one of the most talked-about celebrity events in British tabloid history. The couple secured a reported $5 million deal for the exclusive rights to photograph their wedding, a lavish affair held amid the picturesque backdrop of Italy. This staggering sum underscored the immense public fascination with the pair, whose relationship had captivated Britain since their teenage years together.

The ceremony itself was nothing short of extravagant, with estimates placing the total cost at around $10 million. Among the many memorable details of the celebration was a particularly whimsical touch: as the newlyweds shared their first kiss as husband and wife, guests released cages full of butterflies into the air, creating a fairy-tale moment that was widely captured and circulated in the press. The image became emblematic of the wedding's opulence and theatrical grandeur.

Despite the fairy-tale setting and eye-watering budget, the British media was far from kind in its coverage of the event and the couple themselves. Tabloids and commentators frequently derided the wedding and the pair as "tacky," a characterization that extended into broader, often personal attacks. Rooney, in particular, became a target for cruel jokes about his appearance, earning the unflattering nickname "Shrek" due to comparisons made to the animated ogre. Much of this mockery was intertwined with thinly veiled classism, as critics seized upon his working-class roots in Liverpool as fodder for ridicule, framing his success and wealth as somehow incongruous with his background.

Coleen McLoughlin, for her part, endured her own share of media scrutiny, much of it fixated on her physical appearance and lifestyle choices. Tabloids relentlessly commented on her weight and portrayed her as obsessed with shopping, painting a caricature that often overshadowed her genuine accomplishments. This narrative persisted even as McLoughlin built an impressive career of her own, becoming a millionaire through savvy ventures in media, writing, and advertising endorsements—achievements that demonstrated business acumen rarely acknowledged in the coverage of her.

Yet, despite the barrage of criticism and unflattering headlines, McLoughlin has consistently projected a warmth and authenticity that seems to resonate with the public in more intimate settings. This genuine, relatable quality was particularly evident in her television series "Coleen's Real Women," a program that showcased her down-to-earth personality and connection with everyday people. The show offered audiences a glimpse of McLoughlin beyond the tabloid caricature—revealing someone personable, approachable, and far removed from the one-dimensional portrayal often presented by the press. This contrast between media narrative and personal reality highlights the often unfair and reductive nature of celebrity coverage, particularly for public figures whose backgrounds or successes challenge traditional class expectations.

# The Wedding That Divided a Nation: Rooney, McLoughlin, and the Price of Class Warfare

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin exchanged vows in a fairy-tale ceremony at the Castello di Casiglio in Italy, they weren't just celebrating their union—they were cashing in on it, to the tune of $5 million. The exclusive rights to photograph their reported $10 million wedding were sold to OK! magazine, a deal that would make headlines not just for its staggering figures, but for what it revealed about Britain's enduring obsession with class.

The couple, barely into their twenties at the time, had already become tabloid fixtures long before they said "I do." Rooney, the working-class boy from Croxteth who became one of football's brightest stars, and McLoughlin, his childhood sweetheart turned fashion icon and reality television personality, had spent years under the unforgiving glare of the British press. Their rise from Liverpool's council estates to national celebrity had never been treated as a simple success story—it was persistently framed through a lens of snobbery, with commentators and critics eager to remind the public of their origins.

The wedding itself became a lightning rod for this ongoing scrutiny. Critics were quick to pounce on details that struck them as excessive or, in their words, "tacky"—chief among them a theatrical finale in which butterflies were released into the air as the newlyweds embraced. To detractors, this moment epitomized everything they found distasteful about the couple's aesthetic: over-the-top, sentimental, and lacking the restraint associated with more "traditional" high-society weddings. Newspapers and gossip columns delighted in mocking the spectacle, framing it as proof that money couldn't buy taste.

Yet beneath the mockery lay a more complicated narrative. The sheer scale of the payday—$5 million for photo rights alone—demonstrated that whatever the press thought of their style, the public appetite for the Rooney-McLoughlin brand was undeniable. OK! magazine's willingness to invest such a substantial sum reflected calculated business logic: readers wanted to see this wedding, regardless of what critics said about butterfly releases or opulent excess.

McLoughlin, in particular, became a symbol of this tension. As a young woman from a working-class background who had transformed herself into a savvy entrepreneur and media personality, she often bore the brunt of the classist commentary. Yet she also represented a new kind of celebrity resilience—one that didn't require approval from traditional gatekeepers of taste and style. Her ability to monetize her personal life, build a fashion empire, and maintain public popularity despite constant derision spoke to a broader cultural shift, where authenticity and relatability could triumph over inherited notions of sophistication.

The Rooney-McLoughlin wedding, then, became more than a celebrity event—it evolved into a case study of British class anxieties playing out in real time. The public fascination with the couple, combined with the press's simultaneous scorn and voyeuristic coverage, exposed uncomfortable truths about how social mobility was received in the UK. Success achieved outside traditional upper-class channels was often treated with suspicion, even as it generated massive commercial interest.

Ultimately, the wedding stood as a testament to the couple's ability to navigate—and profit from—a media landscape that seemed determined to diminish them. Whether or not the butterfly release was in poor taste became almost beside the point; what mattered was that Rooney and McLoughlin had turned scrutiny into currency, proving that resilience against snobbery could be as valuable as any five-million-dollar contract.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN opinion piece defending Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin's lavish wedding against British media criticism.
counterfactuals.output:
# In Defense of a Fairy Tale: Why We Should Let Wayne and Coleen Have Their Day

There's something peculiarly British about watching two young people fall in love, achieve extraordinary success, and then criticizing them for enjoying it.

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin married in Portofino, Italy, in a ceremony reportedly costing over £5 million, the response from sections of the British press was swift and predictable: eye-rolling coverage of the excess, the designer gowns, the exclusive magazine deals, the sheer audacity of a footballer and his childhood sweetheart celebrating their union in style.

But let's pause and consider what we're actually criticizing here.

**A Love Story, Not a Scandal**

Wayne and Coleen met as teenagers in Liverpool. They grew up together, weathered tabloid scrutiny before either had reached adulthood, and stayed together through Rooney's meteoric rise from Everton wonderkid to Manchester United and England star. This isn't a manufactured celebrity romance—it's two working-class kids from Croxteth who found each other before the fame arrived and chose to stay together after it did.

Should we really be mocking them for celebrating that journey?

**Earned, Not Given**

Rooney's wealth wasn't inherited or won on a game show. It was earned through extraordinary talent, years of dedication, and a career that put England's footballing hopes on his shoulders from an absurdly young age. Coleen, too, has built her own media and fashion career. If two people who worked hard and achieved success want to spend their own money on a wedding that reflects that success, by what standard are we entitled to judge them?

**The British Discomfort with Success**

There's a peculiar strain in British culture that celebrates achievement right up until someone actually enjoys the fruits of it. We want our working-class heroes to remain humble, to apologize for their wealth, to spend it quietly and self-consciously. When they don't—when they throw a lavish party in an Italian coastal town instead—we brand it as vulgar.

But vulgarity is subjective. Extravagance is relative. What's excessive to a newspaper columnist might simply be a footballer and his bride wanting their wedding photos to look like something out of a storybook.

**The Real Story We're Missing**

Perhaps instead of counting the cost of the flowers or mocking the exclusivity deal with a gossip magazine, we might notice something rather sweet: two people who grew up in the same neighborhood, fell in love before either was famous, and chose to celebrate that with the people who mattered to them, in a place that felt magical.

Sometimes a wedding is just a wedding. Let them have it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a commentary article about the class-based snobbery surrounding a celebrity footballer's wedding, including details about the picture rights deal and charity donations.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wedding Circus: When Snobbery Dresses Up as Cultural Criticism

There's a particular strain of British commentary that emerges every time a footballer gets married, and it's rarely about the couple themselves. It's about the flowers being "too much," the ceremony being "gaudy," the whole affair somehow representing everything wrong with modern celebrity culture. This week's wedding coverage has followed the script perfectly.

## The Real Story Behind the Sneering

Let's be honest about what's actually happening here. A young footballer—working class, extraordinarily talented, and suddenly very wealthy—has done what wealthy people have always done: had an expensive wedding. The difference is that when old money does this, magazines call it "timeless elegance." When new money does it, commentators reach for words like "tacky" and "vulgar."

The picture rights deal has become a particular lightning rod for criticism. Yes, the couple sold exclusive photography rights to a magazine for a substantial sum. This is treated as evidence of crass commercialism, as though it's somehow different from what countless celebrities—including plenty from more socially acceptable backgrounds—have done for decades. Nobody accused certain royals of "selling out" when their wedding photos appeared in carefully curated spreads.

## Where the Money Actually Went

Here's what tends to get buried beneath the snobbery: a significant portion of proceeds from that picture deal reportedly went to charity. Children's hospitals, youth football initiatives, causes tied to the communities these players often came from themselves. This detail rarely makes the headline. It doesn't fit the narrative of footballer-as-tasteless-nouveau-riche that sells papers and generates clicks.

The charitable donation isn't a footnote—it's arguably the most significant part of the story, and its absence from most commentary tells you everything about what this criticism is really about.

## The Class Tell

Strip away the specifics and ask yourself: would a hedge fund manager's £2 million wedding generate this much scorn? Would an aristocrat's elaborate ceremony be picked apart for "bad taste"? The uncomfortable answer is no—because this isn't really about spending, ostentation, or even privacy concerns around commercial photo deals.

It's about who gets to be wealthy without judgment.

Footballers occupy a strange space in British class consciousness. They're paid extraordinarily well for skills that don't require university degrees or the "right" accent. Many come from backgrounds that wouldn't have historically produced this kind of visible wealth. When they spend that money in ways that mirror what the actual aristocracy and old-money elite have always done—elaborate weddings, exclusive media deals, grand gestures—they're mocked for "not knowing how to handle money" or "confusing wealth with class."

## A Different Standard

The genuinely interesting story here isn't the flower arrangements or the reported cost of the venue. It's the charitable giving that accompanied it, the fact that a picture deal—a fairly standard celebrity practice—generated funds for causes that matter. That's a story about someone using newfound wealth and platform responsibly.

Instead, we got columns about vulgarity, thinly-veiled classism dressed up as taste commentary, and precious little acknowledgment that the couple actually did something worth praising.

Perhaps it's time we asked why weddings like this generate more scrutiny than actual issues of wealth inequality, tax arrangements, or corporate excess. The answer, uncomfortably, might be that footballers make an easier target than the people who actually deserve our scrutiny.

---

*What do you think? Is criticism of celebrity weddings really about taste, or something else entirely? Share your thoughts below.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person op-ed for CNN.com discussing how tabloids have mocked a working-class couple's rise to fame, referencing their wedding budget and the media's obsession with their background.
counterfactuals.output:
# I Watched a Couple's Fairytale Turn Into Tabloid Fodder — And It Made Me Sick

There's a particular kind of cruelty reserved for people who dare to succeed without the "right" pedigree.

I've spent years watching how the press covers stories of unexpected success — the shop worker who wins big, the local musician who gets discovered, the couple whose love story captures public imagination. And I've noticed a pattern that should trouble anyone who cares about fairness in media: we love an underdog story right up until the underdog actually wins. Then, suddenly, the same qualities we found charming become targets for ridicule.

Consider how tabloids often treat working-class couples who find themselves thrust into the spotlight. Headlines fixate on wedding budgets with barely concealed sneers — as if love should come with a minimum price tag to be taken seriously. A modest venue becomes "proof" they don't belong in their new social circles. A budget dress becomes a punchline rather than a testament to priorities that value substance over spectacle.

The obsession with background is even more telling. Where did they grow up? What did their parents do for work? Did they attend the "right" schools? These aren't neutral biographical details — they're coded questions designed to answer one thing: *do they deserve this?*

I've watched this play out enough times to recognize the script. The initial coverage is warm, even celebratory — human interest stories about hard work paying off. But inevitably, the tone shifts. Success stories about working-class people succeeding start reading like cautionary tales about people who've "gotten above their station." The language changes from "inspiring" to "surprising" to, eventually, "suspicious."

What strikes me most is the double standard. When wealthy couples have extravagant weddings, it's aspirational content. When working-class couples have modest ones, it's treated as evidence of some fundamental unfitness for their new circumstances. When privileged people succeed, it's expected. When working-class people succeed, it apparently requires explanation, scrutiny, and often mockery.

This isn't really about wedding budgets or hometowns at all. It's about who we've decided gets to have a happy ending without commentary, and who has to defend their right to joy.

I'd like to see coverage that celebrates people for who they are rather than interrogating them for who they aren't. Success shouldn't require an apology for your origins. A wedding's worth isn't measured in dollars spent, and a person's worth in status isn't measured by their parents' occupations.

Maybe it's time tabloid media asked itself a harder question: Why does a working-class success story make us so uncomfortable that we feel compelled to tear it down?

*The author writes on media and culture.*

---

*Note: I've written this as a general op-ed since you didn't specify a particular couple. If you're thinking of a specific news story or public figures, let me know and I can tailor the piece with more specific, accurate details.*

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin exchanged vows in Portofino, Italy, the tabloids were ready with their knives sharpened before the confetti even settled. A reported $5 million deal for exclusive magazine rights. A release of butterflies fluttering into the Italian sky as the couple sealed their union. A guest list stacked with footballers, WAGs, and Manchester United royalty. To critics, it was the epitome of excess—working-class kids playing dress-up as celebrities, trading intimacy for spectacle.

But let's pump the brakes on the pearl-clutching.

**The Money Talk**

Yes, $5 million for magazine rights sounds obscene to anyone outside professional football's stratosphere. But let's be honest about what that deal actually represents: smart business, not tackiness. Rooney and McLoughlin didn't invite paparazzi to hide in bushes and snap grainy photos sold to the highest bidder. They controlled their own narrative, on their own terms, and got compensated for the privacy they were sacrificing anyway. In an era when celebrity weddings are going to be photographed regardless, choosing to profit from that inevitability isn't greed—it's savvy. Would critics prefer they'd given away the images for free while some photographer profited off drone shots?

**Butterflies Aren't a Crime**

Then there's the butterfly release—derided by some as saccharine, over-the-top romanticism unfit for a footballer's wedding. But since when did professional athletes forfeit the right to sentimentality? The butterfly moment wasn't manufactured cynicism; it was a young couple, still in their early twenties, marking a milestone with whimsy. If Kate Middleton had released butterflies at Westminster Abbey, commentators would've called it "enchanting." When Coleen does it, it's "tacky." The double standard says more about class prejudice than actual taste.

**The Real Story: Young Love, Old Money**

What critics are really uncomfortable with isn't the wedding itself—it's who's having it. Rooney, a working-class lad from Croxteth, and McLoughlin, his childhood sweetheart from the same streets, have ascended to wealth most of their detractors will never touch. There's an undercurrent of resentment dressed up as taste-policing: How dare they be this rich, this young, and still throw a party that looks like *they're* enjoying it rather than performing quiet, tasteful restraint?

Weddings are deeply personal expressions of love and identity. Rooney and McLoughlin didn't ask anyone to attend, didn't force anyone to buy the magazine, and didn't harm a single soul by having doves—sorry, butterflies—take flight over the Mediterranean.

Let them have their fairy tale. They earned it.

# Why Are We Still Sneering at Working-Class Joy?

Right, let's have it out then, shall we?

Because the moment photographs emerged from the Rooney-McLoughlin wedding—all fifteen bridesmaids, the ice sculpture shaped like their first family dog, and yes, the fireworks display that reportedly cost more than my house—you could practically hear the collective gasp from certain postcodes. The clutching of pearls. The *tutting*.

"Vulgar," they called it. "Tacky." One particularly vicious columnist (who I shan't dignify by naming, but you know exactly who you are, love) sneered about "council house Cinderella" as if that's meant to be clever rather than just grubby snobbery dressed up in a broadsheet byline.

Let's be honest with ourselves here. If this had been some minor royal or a hedge fund manager's daughter dropping half a million on a wedding, we'd be calling it "tasteful opulence" and "a fairytale celebration." But because it's a lad who grew up on a terraced street and a girl who did her nails at a salon before she made it big, suddenly it's "common." Suddenly it's "try-hard." Suddenly everyone's an expert on what constitutes proper taste.

I'm sorry, but who exactly appointed the class police?

And here's what really gets my goat: nobody's mentioning that this couple, so gleefully mocked for their gold-plated everything, quietly donated £50,000 to the local children's hospice before they'd even sent out invitations. Nobody's talking about the fact that leftover catering—and there was a *lot* of it, because apparently feeding your genuine friends and family properly is now a crime—went straight to a homeless shelter in Manchester. Funny how that never makes the headlines, isn't it? Doesn't fit the narrative of "flashy nouveau riche with more money than sense."

The truth, dear readers, is that this wasn't about taste at all. It was about *who* was allowed to have taste in the first place.

There's a very old, very British disease that flares up whenever working-class people achieve success and dare to enjoy it publicly. We're meant to make our money and then apologise for it—stay humble, stay quiet, buy a nice-but-not-too-nice house, and definitely don't have the audacity to throw a wedding your gran would've dreamed about. God forbid you actually *celebrate* clawing your way up from nothing.

Meanwhile, the aristocracy can spend millions on weddings with actual tiaras rented from the Crown Jewels collection and it's "heritage." It's "elegant." Nobody calls Princess Whoever's third cousin "tacky" for having swans on the lake.

So no, I won't be joining the pile-on. I think it's smashing that two people who scrapped hard for everything they've got decided to throw the party of the century—and gave generously while they were at it. If watching working-class people be happy, generous, and unapologetically *extra* offends your delicate sensibilities, might I suggest the problem isn't the confetti cannons.

It's you.
